summary: Explains how inter-domain multicast routing works when sites use the Locator/ID Separation Protocol. It is an experimental specification covering multicast across LISP and non-LISP boundaries.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains how multicast traffic can cross networks that use LISP address separation. It maps the source's identity to a network locator and carries multicast packets between tunnel routers.

subtitle: How multicast routing works across LISP and non-LISP network sites.

tldr.problem: LISP separates endpoint identifiers from routing locators, while multicast routing must distribute traffic across sites that may use different address spaces.
tldr.mechanism: LISP-Multicast maps multicast source EIDs to RLOCs, uses multicast joins to build state in sites and the core, and encapsulates multicast packets between tunnel routers.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes an Experimental approach that requires no multicast packet-format changes. It identifies areas needing further work, including proxy-ITRs and locator reachability.

today: RFC 6831 is an Experimental RFC published in January 2013. Its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it describes LISP multicast behavior and notes that further experimentation and work would be useful.

sections.title: LISP and Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
LISP uses Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) for endpoints in sites and Routing Locators (RLOCs) for routing through the core. Unicast requires mapping source and destination addresses; multicast requires mapping the source, because the group address is not tied to network topology.

This document describes inter-domain multicast across LISP sites and mixed LISP and non-LISP sites. It focuses on source mapping during multicast tree setup and packet delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: Within a site, a host has an EID. The core routes using RLOCs, so multicast routing needs to translate the source identifier into a locator while keeping the group address.

sections.title: Building a Multicast Distribution Tree
sections.content:
Receivers join multicast groups using their existing host and site mechanisms. An ETR maps a source EID to a locator, then sends join information toward the source-site ITR and into the core for the corresponding source RLOC and group.

The resulting state exists as source-EID and group state inside sites and source-RLOC and group state in the core. When the source sends a packet, an ITR encapsulates it, and routers replicate it along the multicast tree. Receiver-site ETRs decapsulate packets for local receivers.
sections.plainLanguage: Receiver joins help build forwarding state from the source site to the receiver sites. The source-site router adds an outer header, and receiver-site routers remove it before forwarding the packet locally.

sections.title: Protocol and Forwarding Behavior
sections.content:
The RFC describes operational changes for multicast routing protocols, including translating source addresses in join and prune messages as they cross site boundaries. Multicast operation inside a site does not need to change when all sources and receivers are local.

On the data path, the ITR encapsulates the multicast packet and the ETR decapsulates it. The group address is retained in the outer destination, and the inner packet keeps the source EID.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers at site boundaries translate source information when building the tree. They encapsulate packets for the core and restore the original packet at the receiving site.

sections.title: Interworking with Non-LISP Sites
sections.content:
The RFC discusses combinations of LISP, unicast-only LISP, and non-LISP sites. It describes possible proxy roles for supporting communication between LISP multicast sources and sites that do not implement LISP multicast.

It also discusses mixed IPv4 and IPv6 environments. Each multicast tree uses one address family, and the RFC sets conditions on which locators may be grouped by multicast priority.
sections.plainLanguage: A network can contain sites with different LISP capabilities. The RFC describes border mechanisms for making multicast work across those site types and requires each tree to use one IP address family.

sections.title: Security and Areas for Further Work
sections.content:
The RFC says that security considerations are largely those of LISP and multicast. It identifies a possible issue when multiple source EIDs map to one RLOC and share a core multicast tree: receivers could receive traffic for a source they did not join.

The document says the security topic has not been investigated deeply and identifies further work on multicast proxy-ITRs, tracing, and locator reachability.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing one core tree among several source identifiers can cause traffic to reach sites that did not request that exact source. The RFC calls for more work on this and other operational topics.

references.text: Farinacci, D., Fuller, V., Meyer, D., and D. Lewis, "The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP)", RFC 6830, January 2013.
